summary: Gives guidelines for managing IP address space, reviewed by several engineering groups. It describes how address space should be allocated to organizations. It was replaced by RFC 1466.

eli5.summary: Rules for handing out Internet addresses fairly and carefully, so they do not run out too fast.

questions: how were ip addresses allocated in 1992
what is a class c network
subtitle: Guidelines for fairly allocating IP addresses to regions and organizations.

tldr.problem: IP address space is limited and was being consumed quickly in the early Internet. Without a systematic allocation approach, addresses would be wasted and the space would be exhausted.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes dividing Class C IP addresses into eight regional blocks for different geographic areas (Europe, North America, South America, Pacific Rim), with regional registries delegated to manage allocation within their areas, while Class A and B remain centrally managed.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations helped delay IP address exhaustion and paved the way for regional Internet registries. However, the approach was superseded by RFC 1466 and eventually by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) and IPv6.

facts.label: Regional blocks
facts.value: 8 blocks of ~131,000 Class C addresses each

today: RFC 1366 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1466. The classful addressing approach it describes was largely replaced by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) in the mid-1990s, which provided more flexible address allocation. Today, addressing is managed by regional Internet registries descended from the structure proposed here, now handling IPv4 and IPv6.

sections.title: The Problem with Address Distribution
sections.content:
As the Internet grew rapidly in the late 1980s and early 1990s, demand for IP addresses was increasing dramatically. The previous approach of allowing a single central registry (the Internet Registry) to assign all addresses worldwide was becoming a bottleneck. Different regions of the world—Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Americas—had different needs and growth rates, making centralized management inefficient.

This RFC proposes a solution: divide the responsibility for address allocation across regional registries that understand local needs and can respond quickly. It also outlines a systematic approach to allocating address blocks based on organization size and predicts where address space will be used.
sections.eli5: When one person is too busy to give everyone what they need, you split the job. Different people in different places can give out addresses based on what their region needs.

sections.title: IP Address Classes and Their Scarcity
sections.content:
IP addresses at the time were divided into classes. Class A addresses (starting with 1-126) could host millions of devices each but there were only about 126 total—about 77 were unassigned. Class B addresses (starting with 128-191) could host tens of thousands each and had about 16,383 available, with 7,354 already assigned. Class C addresses could host 254 devices each and there were over 2 million available with only about 44,000 assigned.

The RFC recognizes that Class A and B are precious and exhaustible resources that should remain under central control. Class C space, however, is large enough to divide regionally. The highest ranges (208.0.0.0 through 223.255.255.255) are reserved for future use.
sections.eli5: Big address blocks (Class A and B) are rare and should stay controlled by one person. Smaller blocks (Class C) are plenty, so they can be split among different regions.

sections.title: Regional Block Allocation
sections.content:
The RFC proposes dividing the usable Class C space into eight equal blocks, each containing about 131,000 addresses (6% of the total Class C space). These are allocated geographically:

  • Multi-regional: 192.0.0.0 - 193.255.255.255 (for previously assigned addresses)
  • Europe: 194.0.0.0 - 195.255.255.255
  • North America: 198.0.0.0 - 199.255.255.255
  • Central and South America: 200.0.0.0 - 201.255.255.255
  • Pacific Rim: 202.0.0.0 - 203.255.255.255
  • Additional flexibility blocks for unforeseen regions

Regional registries chosen by each geographic area take responsibility for allocating addresses within their block. The Internet Registry remains the root authority and serves regions without designated registries.
sections.eli5: Imagine dividing a pizza into eight slices, one for each region. The person running the registry in that region hands out addresses from their slice.

sections.title: How Organizations Get Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC provides specific rules for how many consecutive Class C addresses an organization receives based on how many they need (based on a 24-month projection):

  • Fewer than 256 addresses needed: 1 Class C network
  • Fewer than 512 addresses: 2 consecutive Class Cs
  • Fewer than 1024 addresses: 4 consecutive Class Cs
  • Fewer than 2048 addresses: 8 consecutive Class Cs
  • Fewer than 4096 addresses: 16 consecutive Class Cs

This approach, called address aggregation, allows multiple small blocks to be combined into larger routing prefixes, reducing the burden on Internet routers. Class A and B requests must still go to the central IANA, with Class B requiring organizations to prove they need more than 4096 addresses and have a proper subnetting plan.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving out individual addresses one at a time, registries give out whole blocks at once. A small company gets one block, a bigger company gets several blocks stuck together.

sections.title: Limitations and What Came After
sections.content:
The RFC frankly acknowledges that these guidelines would only delay address exhaustion, not prevent it indefinitely. Growing numbers of Class C assignments would require routing technology to handle much larger tables of network prefixes. The document notes that further technological changes would be needed to support this growth.

This RFC was replaced by RFC 1466 and has since been superseded by more sophisticated approaches including Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), which allowed flexible address blocks not tied to the A/B/C system. Eventually, IPv6 was deployed to provide a vastly larger address space.
sections.eli5: This plan buys time by being careful about handing out addresses. But it does not fix the problem forever—you still eventually run out of addresses.
